question: Can an indefinite second-order or quasi-Newton search direction be globalized simply by allowing a negative line-search step when the proposed direction points uphill?

key_findings.claim: The proposed Wolfe-plus/minus procedure reduces an ascent direction to an ordinary descent line search by reversing the direction and then negating the returned step.
key_findings.evidence: Algorithm 1 tests the directional derivative. For an ascent direction p it calls a standard Wolfe search on -p and returns the negative of that step, so the actual update alpha p is exactly the positive-step update along -p.

key_findings.claim: Under deterministic smooth optimization assumptions, the sign-generalized Wolfe conditions yield the same Zoutendijk descent bound for ascent directions paired with negative steps.
key_findings.evidence: Proposition 1 assumes a lower-bounded differentiable objective with Lipschitz gradient, directions uniformly nonorthogonal to the gradient, and Wolfe-satisfying nonzero steps. The appendix derives a per-step decrease proportional to cos-squared(theta_k) times the squared gradient norm and concludes the gradient norm tends to zero.

anchors.section: Appendix A definitions and Wolfe conditions

key_findings.claim: Negative steps rescue SR1 from immediate divergence on the reported neural-network training examples, but the evidence is small-scale and iteration-based.
key_findings.evidence: On the heart dataset, full SR1 with positive-only Wolfe steps diverges while SR1 plus Wolfe-plus/minus lowers training error over 50 iterations, with the gap appearing larger for one to three hidden layers. The paper does not report line-search evaluation counts, wall-clock time, held-out performance, or uncertainty for this figure.

key_findings.claim: Limited-memory SR1 with negative steps attains the lowest or tied-lowest training error on many of fourteen tabular tasks, but does not dominate Adam and the damping comparison confounds accuracy with implementation cost.
key_findings.evidence: Table 1 shows l-SR1 plus Wolfe-plus/minus beating or tying Adam on nine datasets by the displayed numbers, while Adam is better on five. Damped l-SR1 fails to finish on three high-feature datasets, but no time limit, hardware, repeat count, standard deviations, test metric, or objective-evaluation budget is supplied.

method.core_idea: Preserve an indefinite second-order method's proposed direction but let the line-search scalar have either sign, choosing the negative ray whenever its directional derivative is positive.
method.mechanism: Wolfe-plus/minus wraps an existing Wolfe line search: use p normally when g-transpose-p is negative, otherwise search along -p and negate the scalar. A sign-adjusted curvature condition then supports the standard Zoutendijk convergence proof.
assumptions: The objective is deterministic, bounded below on the relevant level set, continuously differentiable, and has a Lipschitz-continuous gradient.
Every search direction remains uniformly bounded away from orthogonality with the gradient.
A Wolfe-satisfying line-search step exists on the selected ray and its objective/gradient evaluation cost is acceptable.

techniques.role: Extends a standard Wolfe wrapper to choose between the positive and negative rays of a proposed search direction.
Transfers the classic sufficient-decrease argument to ascent directions paired with negative step sizes.
Uses SR1 curvature estimates without forcing them positive definite, with ray reversal as the globalization mechanism.

evaluations.setting: Heart binary-classification neural networks with one, two, and three hidden layers
evaluations.metric: Training error over at most 50 optimizer iterations
evaluations.result: Full SR1 diverges with positive-only Wolfe steps and converges with Wolfe-plus/minus; the latter ends below BFGS, GD, and Adam in the plotted runs.
evaluations.baseline: GD, Adam, full BFGS, and positive-step full SR1.

evaluations.setting: Fourteen LIBSVM-style tabular datasets fitted with neural networks
evaluations.result: l-SR1 plus Wolfe-plus/minus is best or tied by the table values on nine tasks, while Adam is lower on five; positive-only l-SR1 often remains near chance.
evaluations.baseline: GD, Adam, l-BFGS, positive-step l-SR1, and eigenvalue-damped l-SR1.

evaluations.setting: The same one- to three-hidden-layer heart models
evaluations.metric: Step sign and cosine similarity to steepest descent
evaluations.result: SR1 frequently proposes ascent directions and the wrapper selects negative steps on those iterations.
evaluations.baseline: GD, Adam, and positive-definite BFGS direction/step traces.

limitations: Reviewer inference: the method is exactly a sign flip of the entire proposed direction; it does not isolate or selectively follow individual negative-curvature eigendirections.

Reviewer inference: the convergence theorem is deterministic and assumes uniformly gradient-related directions, conditions not established for noisy minibatch neural-network training or arbitrary SR1 updates.

Reviewer inference: experiments use shallow networks and small/tabular binary datasets, cap the full-method comparison at 50 iterations, and report training error rather than validation or test performance.

Reviewer inference: there are no evaluation-count, wall-clock, hardware, repeated-seed, or uncertainty-controlled comparisons, and the damping baseline's expensive eigendecomposition is implementation-specific.
failure_modes: If an indefinite quasi-Newton direction becomes nearly orthogonal to the gradient, the proof's uniform angle condition fails and sign reversal alone gives little descent.
A negative step reverses every component of the direction, so helpful positive-curvature components may also be reversed together with harmful ones.
Repeated full-batch Wolfe searches can require many objective and gradient evaluations, making favorable iteration counts misleading at modern model scale.
With stochastic minibatches, the measured directional derivative can have the wrong sign and the two rays can be compared using inconsistent noisy objectives.
reusable_insights: Before regularizing an indefinite direction toward the gradient, evaluate whether its opposite ray is already a useful descent direction.
Optimizer comparisons involving line searches should normalize by gradient evaluations and wall-clock time, not just outer iterations.
Separate retaining an indefinite Hessian approximation from selectively exploiting negative curvature; flipping a whole step is not the latter.
State gradient-related angle assumptions explicitly when invoking Zoutendijk-style global convergence.
open_questions: Can Wolfe-plus/minus be made reliable with stochastic gradients using paired batches or confidence tests for the directional-derivative sign?
When does whole-direction reversal outperform eigenspace-selective negative-curvature steps under equal Hessian-vector-product cost?
Does limited-memory SR1 plus negative steps scale to transformers when measured by tokens, wall-clock time, and held-out loss?
Can a line search compare both rays adaptively rather than committing based only on the local directional derivative?

competitive_landscape.title: Identifying and attacking the saddle point problem in high-dimensional non-convex optimization
competitive_landscape.difference: Dauphin et al.'s saddle-free Newton replaces Hessian eigenvalues by their magnitudes, selectively changing curvature signs but requiring costly spectral operations; Wolfe-plus/minus reverses one aggregate SR1 direction without decomposing the Hessian.

competitive_landscape.title: A Newton-MR algorithm with complexity guarantees for nonconvex smooth unconstrained optimization
competitive_landscape.difference: Liu and Roosta use MINRES to detect non-positive curvature and obtain first- and second-order complexity guarantees; the reviewed work supplies a simpler ray-reversal/Zoutendijk result but no saddle-escape or iteration-complexity guarantee.

competitive_landscape.title: On the efficiency of Stochastic Quasi-Newton Methods for Deep Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Yousefi and Martinez extensively compare stochastic limited-memory BFGS and indefinite SR1 across architectures, batches, and sampling choices; Shea and Schmidt contribute the negative-step globalization wrapper and deterministic proof but a narrower empirical study.

competitive_landscape.title: Symmetric Rank-One Quasi-Newton Methods for Deep Learning Using Cubic Regularization
competitive_landscape.difference: Ranganath et al. retain indefinite limited-memory SR1 and solve adaptively regularized cubic subproblems with closed-form structure; Wolfe-plus/minus avoids that subproblem but provides weaker curvature-specific guarantees and comparisons.

novelty_assessment: Author claim: negative step sizes are a largely unexplored, inexpensive way to preserve second-order curvature information while globalizing ascent-producing methods. Reviewer inference after primary-source comparison: preserving negative curvature through saddle-free Newton, trust-region, MINRES, and indefinite SR1 was well established. The distinct contribution is the minimal Wolfe wrapper and its sign-symmetric Zoutendijk proof. Because a negative step along p is exactly a positive step along -p, the conceptual novelty is narrower than the framing suggests, and the paper does not show competitive modern-scale efficiency.
reviewer_notes: Read all twelve extracted pages, including the convergence proof, pseudocode, all tables/figures, and experimental appendix. I recomputed the table win/tie count from displayed training errors and distinguish outer-iteration behavior from unreported evaluation and wall-clock cost. Four primary arXiv competitor records, including a subsequent direct SR1 alternative, were checked on 2026-08-23.
